pages.title: Start here: how this workspace runs

text.text: A small food maker answers to three people: the customer who wants the order on time, the inspector who wants every lot traceable, and the owner who wants to know what a jar really costs. This workspace keeps all three in one place.
The four tables
Batches

: one row per production run with its lot code, units made, ingredient, packaging and labor cost, finished pH and the release checks. Status runs Planned, In production, QA hold, Released or Rejected. Release lot stamps the day.
Products

: each product and size, its process (acidified hot fill, high-sugar preserve, bake, refrigerated), allergens, wholesale and retail price. It averages the cost per unit of released lots into a real Wholesale margin.
Ingredients and packaging
: produce, dry goods, oils, sweeteners, jars, lids and labels, with supplier approval, certificate expiry, allergen and reorder point.
Wholesale orders
: grocery, distributor, market, gift shop and online orders with value, ship-by date and the lot codes shipped.
A normal week
Monday: plan the week's batches from open orders and stock. Work the Order this week list.
Each production day: the kitchen lead opens the batch, presses Assign to me, and fills the batch record as they go.
Acidified products: pH is read on a cooled sample. Above 4.6 the lot is Rejected; never re-labelled.
The next morning QA checks labels, allergen statement and retained samples, then presses Release lot.
Orders are packed oldest lot first, the lot codes written in, and Mark shipped pressed at the dock.
Who owns what
Allergens
Granola carries tree nuts and wheat; the dressing carries sesame, soy and wheat. Allergen products run last in the day, followed by a full clean before any other product.

pages.title: Lot tracing and a mock recall

text.text: If a supplier calls about a bad ingredient, or a customer reports a problem, you must say within hours which lots used it and where every jar went. This page is how the kitchen keeps that chain whole, and the twice-yearly mock recall that proves it.
The chain

cells.text: The batch record, written at weigh-up
Lot code on the batch, printed on every jar
Which lots went to which buyer
Lot codes shipped on each wholesale order
Two jars per lot on the sample shelf for the shelf life

text.text: Lot codes
Our code is product prefix plus a running number: SAL for tomato salsa, VER for salsa verde, JAM, GRA, DRS. The number comes from the production calendar, so codes never repeat.
Running a mock recall (90 minutes, twice a year)
Pick one ingredient lot at random, for example a case of pecans.
From its batch records, list every batch that used it.
Open Wholesale orders and find every order whose Lot codes shipped includes those lots.
Count the units: made, shipped, still in the warehouse, retained samples. They must add up.
Write the time it took and anything missing in this page. Two hours is our ceiling; anything slower means a gap in the records to fix this week.
When it is real
Stop shipping the affected lots at once: move any open order holding them back to Confirmed.
Call each buyer the same day with lot codes and units.
Keep a log of every call, time and person.
Rejected or recalled product is held and destroyed with a witness, never reworked into another lot.
Checklist after each batch
Every ingredient's supplier lot written in the batch record
Lot code printed and readable on the first and last jar
Retained samples labelled and shelved
Units made entered so traceback totals add up

pages.title: Costing a jar and setting wholesale price

text.text: Small food makers lose money quietly: a label price creeps up, a batch yields fewer jars, a distributor asks for 25 percent off. This page shows how the workspace turns real batches into a true cost per unit and how to use it when pricing.
What goes into cost per unit
Ingredients at what you paid, including spoilage and trim.
Packaging: jar, lid, label, shrink band and the case.
Labor: hours on the line, including set-up and clean-down, at a loaded hourly rate.

Each batch divides the three by Units made. Products then average the cost of released lots only, so a rejected kettle does not hide inside a good average; it shows as a loss on the Batches chart instead.
Worked example: smoky tomato salsa
A distributor usually takes about 25 percent from the store's price, and the store needs its own margin. That is why we want at least 50 percent at wholesale for anything sold through a distributor.
Monthly price check
Open Products and read Average unit cost and Wholesale margin.
Any product under 45 percent: check the last three batches for yield (units made) and supplier prices on Ingredients and packaging.
Fix yield first: a kettle that fills 560 jars instead of 600 costs more than a five-cent price rise. Weigh the kettle before filling and note the fill weight of the first jar.
Only then raise the wholesale price, with 60 days' notice to buyers.
Rules
Never price from a recipe spreadsheet; price from released batches
Re-check margin when any packaging item changes supplier
Rejected lots are reviewed every month for their cause
Labor hours include set-up and clean-down, not only kettle time
